titleBlock.headline: Taurine Deficiency as a Conserved Driver of Aging: Restoration Extends Lifespan and Primate Healthspan
titleBlock.authors: Singh, P., Gollapalli, K., Mangiola, S., Schranner, D., Yusuf, M.A., Chamoli, M., Shi, S.L., Lopes Bastos, B., Kurup, T., Parra, E.R., ... Wackerhage, H., Lithgow, G.J., Suh, Y., Lamming, D.W., Münzberg, H., Karsenty, G. & Yadav, V.K.
titleBlock.summary: Circulating blood taurine concentrations decline by ~80% between youth and old age in humans, monkeys, and mice. Supplementing middle-aged (14-month-old) C57BL/6J mice with 1,000 mg/kg/day taurine restored youthful blood levels, extending median lifespan by 10% (males) to 12% (females) and remaining life expectancy at 28 months by 18% to 25%, while 6 months of taurine in middle-aged rhesus monkeys improved bone density, metabolic control, liver health, and immune rejuvenation.

studyOverview.title: The Question
studyOverview.content: Taurine (2-aminoethanesulfonic acid) is one of the most abundant semi-essential amino sulfonic acids in mammalian tissues, yet its circulating levels fall precipitously with age. Is this decline merely a passive bystander of aging, or is taurine deficiency an active, reversible driver of systemic aging?

studyOverview.title: What They Did
studyOverview.content: Measured longitudinal/cross-sectional blood taurine across mice, rhesus monkeys, and humans; conducted lifespan trials in C. elegans, yeast, and middle-aged C57BL/6J mice (14 months old, fed 500 or 1,000 mg/kg/day taurine); performed a 6-month randomized trial in 15-year-old rhesus macaques (250 mg/kg/day); and analyzed 11,966 humans in EPIC-Norfolk alongside an acute exercise intervention.

studyOverview.title: What They Found
studyOverview.content: Taurine levels dropped by >80% in aged humans vs. young children/adults. Oral taurine (T1000) extended worm lifespan by +10–23% and mouse median lifespan by +10% (♂) and +12% (♀)—plus +18–25% life expectancy at 28 months—while suppressing cellular senescence, DNA damage (γH2AX), mitochondrial tRNA Leu(UUR) defects, and inflammaging. In 11,966 humans, higher taurine/hypotaurine tracked with lower BMI, T2D, hypertension, and CRP, and acute endurance/sprint exercise significantly boosted blood taurine.

speciesModels.metricLabel: Overall Median Lifespan Gain (+18–25% Life Expectancy at 28 mo)
findings: Extended median lifespan from 29.0 to 32.6 months in females (+12%) and by +10% in males; life expectancy at 28 months rose by 18–25%.
Attenuated age-related weight gain in females (+10% higher energy expenditure via oxygen consumption without altering food intake).
Increased bone mass (BV/TV) and femoral bone strength, neuromuscular coordination (rotarod), grip strength, and reduced anxiety/depression-like behavior.

Reduced p16INK4a+ senescent cells (confirmed via p16-luc reporter mice), lowered γH2AX DNA damage, and restored mitochondrial Complex I activity via taurine-modified mitochondrial tRNALeu(UUR) (5-taurinomethyluridine).
Prevented age-associated weight gain (-0.75 kg vs. control) and reduced visceral fat percentage.
Increased lumbar spine and leg bone mineral density (BMD) and serum osteocalcin while lowering bone resorption marker CTX.
Lowered fasting blood glucose (-19%), reduced hepatic transaminases (AST -36%, ALT -20%), and lowered serum lipid peroxides by -33%.
Rejuvenated the immune compartment by reducing circulating pro-inflammatory monocytes and granulocytes.
Serum taurine levels in 60-year-old humans were ~80% lower than in 5-year-old individuals (~30 µM vs. ~130–150 µM).

Across 11,966 EPIC-Norfolk participants, higher circulating taurine, hypotaurine, and N-acetyltaurine significantly associated with lower BMI, abdominal obesity, Type 2 Diabetes prevalence, fasting glucose, liver enzymes (AST/ALT), and hs-CRP.
A single bout of graded cycling to exhaustion significantly elevated serum taurine (+16% to +25%) and hypotaurine across sedentary adults, sprinters, endurance runners, and natural bodybuilders.
Notably, taurine did NOT extend replicative lifespan in unicellular budding yeast (S. cerevisiae), which lacks taurine biosynthetic/transport dependence.
Extended median and maximum C. elegans lifespan by 10% to 23% in a dose-dependent manner across multiple independent replicates.
Confirmed that taurine's pro-longevity action is evolutionarily conserved across multicellular metazoans.

hallmarksImpacted.mechanism: Taurine is required to synthesize 5-taurinomethyluridine (τm5U) on mitochondrial tRNALeu(UUR), enabling proper translation of ND6 and Complex I subunits; restoring taurine rescued Complex I activity and cut ROS.
In aged p16-luc mice, taurine supplementation suppressed whole-body p16INK4a bioluminescence and protected telomerase-deficient (Terc-/-) mice from premature mortality.
Increased Lgr5+ intestinal crypt stem cells and Pax7+ skeletal muscle satellite cells in aged mice, accelerating tissue regeneration after injury.
Elevated LC3-II/LC3-I ratio and reduced p62 accumulation across liver, brown adipose, and muscle while blunting ER stress (CHOP) and DNA damage (γH2AX).

keyFindings.title: 80% Age-Related Decline in Human Circulating Taurine
keyFindings.desc: Hepatic cysteinesulfinic acid decarboxylase (CSAD)—the rate-limiting enzyme for endogenous taurine synthesis—declines with age, causing an ~80% drop in human serum taurine by age 60.

keyFindings.title: +10–12% Median Lifespan & +18–25% Late-Life Expectancy in Mice
keyFindings.desc: Initiating 1,000 mg/kg/day taurine at 14 months of age extended median survival in both sexes and expanded multi-organ healthspan (bone, muscle, brain, pancreas, gut, and immune system).

keyFindings.title: Primate Translation in Rhesus Macaques
keyFindings.desc: Six months of oral taurine (250 mg/kg/day) in middle-aged monkeys increased lumbar bone density, lowered fasting glucose by 19%, reduced liver transaminases, and suppressed lipid peroxidation by 33%.

keyFindings.title: Exercise Acutely Mobilizes Endogenous Taurine in Humans
keyFindings.desc: Both endurance and sprint exercise significantly increase circulating taurine and hypotaurine in humans, suggesting taurine mediates part of the systemic metabolic benefit of physical activity.

conclusions.title: Causality Proven via Genetic Knockout (Slc6a6) & Supplementation
conclusions.content: Whereas genetic loss of the taurine transporter (Slc6a6-/-) accelerates skeletal muscle, retinal, cardiac, and bone aging and shortens lifespan, middle-aged replenishment reverses these hallmarks and extends mammalian survival.

conclusions.title: Mitochondrial tRNA Modification Links Taurine to Bioenergetics
conclusions.content: Unlike generic antioxidants, taurine plays a structural biochemical role by conjugating to mitochondrial tRNALeu(UUR) to permit translation of electron transport chain Complex I proteins.

conclusions.title: Pending Long-Term Randomized Human Clinical Trials
conclusions.content: While EPIC-Norfolk (n = 11,966), primate RCTs, and short-term human metabolic trials strongly support safety and cardiometabolic benefit, dedicated multi-year human aging trials (using 3–6 g/day taurine) are warranted to confirm long-term epigenetic and functional endpoints.

protocolImplications: Translational context: Allometric scaling of the effective mouse (1,000 mg/kg/day) and rhesus monkey (250 mg/kg/day) doses corresponds to approximately 3 to 6 grams/day of oral taurine in adult humans—within the European Food Safety Authority (EFSA) established safe upper intake level of 6 g/day (100 mg/kg/day). Furthermore, high-intensity interval and endurance exercise naturally stimulate endogenous taurine and hypotaurine biosynthesis.
